items.title: Three children and teacher killed in US primary school shooting
items.tldr: A 16‑year‑old gunman opened fire at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, killing three young students and a teacher before being shot dead by a bystander. Two additional victims, a seven‑year‑old and the teacher, remain in critical condition, prompting nationwide grief and renewed debate over school safety and gun policy.
items.background: The incident marks one of the deadliest school shootings in recent U.S. history, occurring amid an already heightened national conversation about firearm access, mental‑health resources, and the effectiveness of existing safety protocols. In the past year, the K‑12 School Shooting Database recorded 235 shooting incidents across American schools, underscoring a persistent threat to educational environments. The community of Bend, a city of roughly 100,000 residents, is still processing the shock, with schools slated to remain closed through Friday to allow for mourning and security assessments.

analysis.heading: Immediate Response and Law Enforcement Actions
analysis.content: Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz reported that the suspect forced entry by shooting at locked classroom doors, exploiting a vulnerability in the school’s locking mechanism. A civilian who witnessed the chaos pursued the attacker into the building and used his personal firearm to neutralize the threat, a rare example of armed citizen intervention. Police arrived three minutes later, confirming the suspect’s death and conducting a sweep of the campus. The rapid response highlights both the critical importance of situational awareness and the contentious debate over the role of armed bystanders in active‑shooter scenarios.

analysis.heading: Impact on School Safety Policy and Community
analysis.content: Local officials have announced a comprehensive review of security infrastructure, focusing on door‑locking systems, surveillance, and emergency communication. The school had installed new classroom doors in 2022 that could be locked with a switch, yet the shooter was able to breach them, suggesting that hardware alone is insufficient without robust training and rapid response protocols. Community leaders, including school district superintendent Steven Cook, have emphasized the need for mental‑health support and threat‑assessment teams. The tragedy also reignites legislative discussions at both state and federal levels regarding background‑check expansions, red‑flag laws, and potential funding for school safety technology.

analysis.heading: Broader Societal Implications and Potential AI/Technology Interventions
analysis.content: Beyond the immediate loss, the shooting underscores systemic challenges in preventing gun violence in the United States. Analysts point to the intersection of easily accessible firearms, gaps in early‑intervention mental‑health services, and the cultural prevalence of armed responses. In the technology sector, the incident has sparked renewed interest in AI‑driven risk analytics and predictive policing tools that could identify potential threats before they materialize. Companies such as OpenAI, Gemini, and Anthropic are being asked to collaborate on developing ethical AI frameworks for threat detection, while policymakers consider regulation of such systems to balance privacy and safety. The debate reflects broader editorial priorities that emphasize agentic AI, LLM safety, and open‑source regulation, suggesting that emerging technologies may play a role in reshaping how schools safeguard students.

key_facts: The shooter was a 16‑year‑old local boy; his identity has not been released.
Three victims were identified as a five‑year‑old, an eight‑year‑old, and an 11‑year‑old; a seven‑year‑old and a 54‑year‑old teacher are in critical condition.
The suspect was shot dead by a community member who pursued him into the school.
Police were alerted at 12:59 p.m. local time; the first call reported gunfire directed at a car outside the school.
Silver Rail Elementary School serves about 450 students and has over 40 adult staff members.
The K‑12 School Shooting Database recorded 235 incidents in the previous year and at least 140 so far in 2026.
implications: Potential legislative reforms on background checks, red‑flag laws, and school‑safety funding.
Increased scrutiny of physical security measures, including door‑locking systems and emergency communication.
Heightened public debate over armed civilian intervention and the role of law enforcement in active‑shooter situations.
Accelerated interest in AI‑driven threat detection and predictive analytics for educational settings, prompting regulatory discussions.
items.outlook: In the weeks ahead, Bend’s school district is expected to implement a multi‑layered safety plan that combines upgraded physical infrastructure, enhanced staff training, and mental‑health outreach. At the national level, lawmakers may push for bipartisan gun‑policy measures, though historic polarization suggests any consensus will be incremental. Meanwhile, technology firms and AI researchers are likely to be called upon to develop transparent, ethically‑grounded tools for threat assessment, with oversight from bodies such as the U.S. Department of the Treasury and the Federal Aviation Administration to ensure compliance with emerging regulation frameworks. The long‑term impact on student safety, community trust, and the broader discourse on firearm control remains to be seen.

items.fulltext:
Three children and teacher killed in US primary school shooting
- Published
A 16-year-old has shot dead three children and a teacher at a primary school in the US state of Oregon before he was killed by a bystander, police said.
The suspect, who has not been named, forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary School in the city of Bend on Thursday afternoon by shooting at locked doors, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.
The teenager was shot dead by a community member who "pursued him into the school and engaged him", Krantz said.
The three children killed were aged five, eight and 11. A seven-year-old and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to a hospital in a critical condition, Krantz said. It is unclear if the attacker had any links to the school.
"We are stunned and heartbroken by this senseless tragedy," Steven Cook, the top administrative official of the local school district, said in a statement.
"No words can adequately express the grief our community is experiencing."
Police said the attacker was a local 16-year-old boy, but they did not release any further details on him or the identity of the victims.
Police were alerted to an active shooter at Silver Rail Elementary at 12:59 local time, Bend Police Department spokeswoman Sheila Miller told reporters.
The first call came from a person who said that an unknown suspect was shooting into their car with a long gun, police said. Photos released from the scene show a red truck with bullet holes.
Minutes later, the local county dispatch received 911 calls reporting that the attacker had entered the school.
Police said he shot at locks on the doors in order to force his way inside.
Local media reports suggested the school received new classroom doors in 2022 which can be locked with the flip of a switch.
A bystander saw the shooting begin to unfold, pursued the attacker into the school and shot him dead, police said.
Three minutes later, officers first arrived at the scene. They confirmed that the attacker had been killed, and then searched the school.
Schools in Bend have been closed on Friday. Officials said the community needed time to heal.
Around 450 children attend Silver Rail Elementary School, which has more than 40 adult staff members, police said.
According to the K-12 School Shooting Database, there were 235 shooting incidents at American schools last year and at least 140 so far this year.

items.title: 'It's really hard to believe' - How Oregon primary school shooting unfolded
items.tldr: A 16-year-old gunman killed three children and a teacher at a primary school in Bend, Oregon, before being shot dead by an armed community member. Two other students and a teacher remain in critical condition, prompting renewed debate over school safety, gun control, and mental‑health interventions in the United States.
items.background: The tragedy occurred at a crowded elementary school in the Pacific Northwest, a region that has seen a surge in school‑shooting incidents over the past decade. The suspect forced entry by firing at locked classroom doors, indicating a premeditated attack. An armed member of the community—identified as a local resident with a concealed‑carry permit—pursued the shooter and exchanged fire, resulting in the suspect’s death. This use of civilian force raises legal and ethical questions about the role of armed citizens in active‑shooter scenarios. The incident follows a series of high‑profile mass shootings that have intensified the national conversation about gun legislation, mental‑health resources, and school security infrastructure. While Oregon has some of the nation’s stricter gun‑control laws, loopholes surrounding background checks for private sales and the availability of high‑capacity magazines remain contentious. The community’s immediate response, including vigils and calls for action, reflects a broader societal fatigue with recurring violence.

analysis.heading: Tactical Response and Community Armed Intervention
analysis.content: The shooter’s method—firing at locked doors—suggests a tactical intent to breach the school quickly, exploiting potential delays in emergency response. The armed community member’s intervention aligns with the "good guy with a gun" narrative often cited in debates over concealed‑carry policies. However, the chaotic nature of active‑shooter situations means that civilian involvement can also increase risk of accidental shootings, misidentification, and secondary injuries. Law‑enforcement agencies are increasingly emphasizing "run, hide, fight" protocols, but the presence of armed civilians complicates coordination. This case will likely be studied by police training units and school safety committees to refine evacuation drills and communication strategies during incursions.

analysis.heading: Policy and Legislative Implications in the U.S. Gun Debate
analysis.content: The Oregon shooting adds fuel to an already heated legislative arena. Proponents of stricter gun control argue that the tragedy underscores the need for universal background checks, red‑flag laws that allow temporary removal of firearms from individuals deemed dangerous, and the elimination of gun‑free‑zone exemptions. Conversely, Second‑Amendment advocates stress mental‑health screening and swift intervention rather than restricting law‑abiding citizens’ rights. The incident may catalyze bipartisan momentum in the Oregon legislature to tighten permit‑to‑purchase requirements and enhance funding for school resource officers and mental‑health counselors. Nationally, the event could influence the agenda of the upcoming Congressional session, potentially reviving stalled proposals such as the Bipartisan Background Checks Act and the Extreme Risk Protection Order legislation.

analysis.heading: Geopolitical and Societal Ramifications
analysis.content: Mass shootings in the United States have diplomatic overtones, affecting the country’s soft power and global perception of safety and governance. International partners often cite such incidents when critiquing U.S. domestic policy, using them as leverage in trade or security negotiations. Moreover, the frequency of school shootings correlates with heightened public anxiety, which can impact tourism, real‑estate values, and investor confidence in affected regions. The tragedy also highlights disparities in how different communities respond to trauma—some rallying around gun‑control advocacy, others emphasizing constitutional rights. Sociologically, the event deepens existing divides and may influence voter turnout in upcoming elections, as citizens prioritize candidates with clear stances on public safety and mental‑health funding.

key_facts: Four fatalities: three children (ages 5, 8, 11) and one teacher were killed.
The 16‑year‑old shooter forced entry by firing at locked classroom doors.
An armed community member shot and killed the suspect inside the school.
Two additional victims—a 7‑year‑old student and another teacher—are in critical condition at a local hospital.
implications: Potential enactment of stricter background‑check and red‑flag legislation in Oregon and at the federal level.
Reevaluation of school safety protocols, including the role of armed civilians and coordination with law enforcement.
Increased funding and focus on mental‑health services and crisis intervention programs in educational settings.
Heightened public pressure on legislators, likely influencing the next election cycle’s policy platforms.
items.outlook: In the immediate term, lawmakers are expected to introduce emergency measures such as enhanced background checks and temporary firearm restrictions for minors. Over the longer horizon, the incident may spur nationwide adoption of advanced security technologies—AI‑driven threat detection, improved door‑locking mechanisms, and integrated emergency communication systems. Simultaneously, community‑based resilience programs and expanded mental‑health outreach could mitigate the risk of future tragedies, though sustained political will will be essential to translate momentum into lasting reform.

items.title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
items.tldr: BBC Verify analysis shows a record 12 vessels were struck in the Strait of Hormuz during 5‑11 October, the highest weekly tally since the US‑Israel war with Iran began. The surge has cut daily oil flow through the strait to 12.6 million barrels, down from 15 million, and left two Indian sailors missing. Experts say Tehran is escalating attacks to assert control as the US steps up naval escort missions.
items.background: The Strait of Hormuz, a choke point for roughly one‑third of global oil shipments, has long been a flashpoint in the US‑Israel war with Iran that erupted in February 2024. Since then, maritime incidents have fluctuated, but the past week marks an unprecedented spike. The UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency, which collates reports from commercial vessels, recorded 12 attacks in seven days—surpassing the previous weekly high of ten. The escalation coincides with a US Navy initiative to increase the number of escorted tankers through the southern part of the strait, a move intended to protect commercial traffic but which Tehran views as a provocation. The strategic waterway’s importance is underscored by its pre‑war baseline of about 17 million barrels per day, a figure that has not been reached since the conflict began.

analysis.heading: Escalating Iranian Tactics
analysis.content: Iran’s maritime strategy appears to have shifted from sporadic, low‑profile incidents to a near‑daily campaign of strikes. According to Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, Tehran has “evolved its strategy” and is now conducting “multiple attacks every single day.” The attacks are not limited to the strait itself; recent incidents include a drone‑struck tanker north of Qatar (over 500 km from the strait) and a vessel hit near the UAE’s Al‑Jazirah al‑Hamra. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has publicly declared that strikes will not be “limited to the Strait of Hormuz” and has announced a “new deployment formation” across the region, signaling a broader operational reach.

analysis.heading: Impact on Global Oil Markets
analysis.content: Industry data from Kpler reveals that oil throughput through the strait fell to 12.6 million barrels per day on 13 October, down from 15 million at the end of September and well below the pre‑war baseline of 17 million. The decline is driven by two factors: the heightened risk premium on tanker insurance and the adoption of a “shuttle” system where smaller tankers load cargo in the Gulf and transfer to larger vessels in the Gulf of Oman to avoid the most dangerous stretch. While this shuttle method has helped keep some flow moving, it adds cost and logistical complexity. The slowdown has ripple effects on oil‑dependent economies, especially in Asia, and raises concerns about energy security ahead of the winter heating season.

analysis.heading: Strategic Responses from the US and Allies
analysis.content: US Central Command (Centcom) has emphasized that “commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with coordinated protection from US forces and regional partners.” The US Navy’s assisted transit program, which saw an 85 % increase in the number of vessels receiving navigation assistance during the first ten days of October compared with the same period in August, is a direct response to the surge. Regional partners such as Oman and the United Arab Emirates have offered limited cooperation, but Iran continues to accuse them of facilitating the US‑led escort missions. Meanwhile, the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has called for de‑escalation, warning that unchecked attacks could jeopardize global trade and humanitarian shipping.

key_facts: Twelve vessels reported attacks between 5‑11 October, the highest weekly total since the US‑Israel war with Iran began.
Six attacks occurred on a single day (Sunday, 8 October), including the fire‑damaged Petro Dolphin tanker near Sohar Anchorage, Oman.
Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued; two remain missing after the Petro Dolphin incident.
Daily oil flow through the strait dropped to 12.6 million barrels on 13 October, down from 15 million at the end of September.
US Navy assisted transits rose 85 % in early October compared with the same period in August.
implications: Potential upward pressure on global oil prices and increased volatility in energy markets.
Higher insurance premiums and re‑routing costs for shipping companies, possibly reshaping trade logistics.
Escalation risks broader regional conflict, drawing in additional naval forces from other powers.
Humanitarian concerns as civilian crews become collateral damage and missing persons cases rise.
items.outlook: If the current pattern persists, the Strait of Hormuz could become a permanent high‑risk corridor, prompting a structural shift toward alternative routes such as the Suez Canal or the Cape of Good Hope for a portion of oil shipments. The US and its allies may need to sustain or expand escort operations, while diplomatic channels will be critical to prevent inadvertent escalation. Iran’s strategy appears aimed at coercing the international community into recognizing its maritime claims, but the economic fallout could ultimately undermine its own export revenues. Monitoring of Iranian naval deployments and the effectiveness of assisted transit programs will be essential indicators of whether the recent surge is a temporary spike or the start of a sustained campaign.

items.fulltext:
Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
- Published
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.
Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.
Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.
As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.
BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.
Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.
Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.
The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".
Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacks
The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.
The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.
Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.
Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".
Oil shipments stall
Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.
About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.
The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.
Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.
These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.
So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.
Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day".
"The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.
The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.
Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.
A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.
Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.
Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship.
Additional reporting by Becky Dale
Graphics by Tom Shiel and Mark Edwards

items.title: Banks say Healey is planning Budget tax raid on their profits
items.tldr: Senior banking executives anticipate a tax increase in Chancellor John Healey's upcoming Budget, targeting record profits. The UK Finance trade body warns higher taxes could hurt competitiveness, while analysts see a possible surcharge restoration and a moratorium on loss offsetting as likely measures.
items.background: The UK banking sector recorded collective profits of roughly £15 bn in the first six months of 2026, prompting renewed debate over fiscal policy. Chancellor John Healey has praised banks as "crown jewels" of the economy but has left the door open to additional levies. The current regime includes a 3 % surcharge on top of the 25 % corporation tax and a separate bank levy (0.1 % on short‑term loans, 0.05 % on longer‑dated loans, excluding mortgages). Under Rishi Sunak, the surcharge was cut from 8 % while corporation tax was raised from 19 % to 25 %. The sector contributed nearly £40 bn to the Treasury in 2025 when employee income tax is included, and the levy and surcharge together generated £2.6 bn. Banks have historically argued that higher taxes risk eroding the UK’s competitive edge, reducing lending capacity and ultimately harming growth. The last Budget spared the sector, surprising many given the surge in profitability driven by higher interest rates and wider net interest margins.

analysis.heading: Fiscal Impact Assessment
analysis.content: Analysts estimate that restoring the 3 % surcharge to its pre‑Sunak level could raise around £2 bn annually, while a targeted moratorium on the use of past losses to offset current profits could add a further £1 bn per year. The Treasury is also considering adjustments to the bank levy thresholds and possibly extending the levy to include certain off‑balance‑sheet exposures. Such measures would directly address the £15 bn profit surge, but they also risk altering the sector’s risk‑pricing behavior, especially if banks anticipate a tighter fiscal environment.

analysis.heading: Competitive Implications
analysis.content: UK Finance has warned that "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode." International banks, notably JP Morgan, have echoed this concern, with CEO Jamie Dimon cautioning that the UK already carries one of the highest tax burdens on banks globally. A tax hike that spares foreign banks operating in the UK could create an uneven playing field, potentially driving capital toward jurisdictions with more favourable tax regimes, undermining the government’s goal of positioning the UK as a premier financial hub.

analysis.heading: Political Dynamics
analysis.content: Healey’s rhetoric frames banks as essential to the UK’s economic success, yet the political pressure to capture a larger share of windfall profits is strong. Trade unions and advocacy groups have called for additional levies, arguing that the sector’s profitability should contribute more to public services. Any tax increase must balance fiscal needs with the risk of dampening investment, a calculus that will be scrutinized by markets, investors, and the broader public ahead of the Budget.

key_facts: The four largest UK banks generated about £15 bn in profit in H1 2026.
Current bank tax regime: 3 % surcharge + 25 % corporation tax + asset‑based levy.
Bank levy and surcharge together contributed £2.6 bn to the Treasury in 2025.
Restoring the surcharge to 8 % could raise roughly £2 bn per year.
A moratorium on loss‑carry‑back could add an estimated £1 bn annually.
UK Finance warns higher taxes could hurt competitiveness and investment.
JP Morgan’s Jamie Dimon cautions the UK already has one of the highest bank tax burdens worldwide.
implications: Potential reduction in banks’ lending capacity if tax burden rises, possibly tightening credit for households and businesses.
Shift of financial activity to other jurisdictions if UK tax regime becomes relatively less attractive.
Increased fiscal revenue for the Treasury, enabling greater spending on public services or debt reduction.
Political fallout depending on how the tax measures are framed—balancing public demand for fairness against business concerns.
items.outlook: The Chancellor’s Budget later this month is expected to include a mix of targeted tax adjustments aimed at capturing a portion of the banking sector’s recent windfall while attempting to preserve the UK’s status as a competitive financial centre. Markets will watch for any signals on the durability of the surcharge and the treatment of loss‑offset rules. If the measures are perceived as balanced, they could bolster public confidence in fiscal fairness without triggering a significant exodus of banking capital. Conversely, overly aggressive taxation could dampen investment, slow economic growth, and invite criticism from both industry and international observers.

items.fulltext:
Banks say Healey is planning Budget tax raid on their profits
- Published
Senior banking executives have told the BBC they expect the sector to be "on the menu" when the chancellor announces his Budget in two weeks' time.
John Healey has described the banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, yet has refused to rule out a raid on the sector.
The biggest four banks collectively made around Â£15bn profit in the first six months of this year, leading to calls from trade unions and others for additional taxes.
However, the banking sector trade body, UK Finance, warned that "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode".
The UK's biggest banks and building societies currently pay a surcharge of 3% on top of the baseline 25% rate of corporation tax, plus a levy on the assets held on their balance sheets.
The sector contributed nearly Â£40bn to the Treasury last year, if income tax on employees is factored in.
The bank levy generated Â£1.4bn last year and the surcharge a further Â£1.2bn.
There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector.
The 3% surcharge was reduced from 8% under Rishi Sunak, at the same time as he raised corporation tax from 19% to 25%. Returning the surcharge to its previous level could raise around Â£2bn a year.
The bank levy currently charges 0.1% on outstanding short-term loans and 0.05% on longer-dated loans, although mortgages are excluded from the calculation.
In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth.
In truth, banks were pleasantly surprised they were not hit at the last Budget, given the large profits they have been making in recent years. Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which they lend to customers and the rate they pay savers.
There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since.
Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra Â£1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive.
It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.
However, industry leaders say any form of tax rise that hits UK banks and exempts foreign banks' operations in the UK would be hard to square with the government's push to back British business.
Whatever form it takes, banks believe the chancellor now has much more of an appetite to take a larger slice of their pie.

items.title: Equality watchdog writes to Greens over ‘Zionism is racism’ motion
items.tldr: The Equality and Human Rights Commission has asked the Green Party of England and Wales for details on a conference motion that labels Zionism as racism, prompting accusations of antisemitism and a potential breach of the Equality Act. Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs, alongside Jewish groups, warn the motion could jeopardise coalition arrangements and trigger legal action.
items.background: In March 2024 the Green Party’s national conference adopted a motion describing Zionism as an ideology that seeks an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion or domination of non‑Jewish residents. The wording sparked immediate backlash from Jewish organisations, several Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs, and the Campaign Against Antisemitism, who argued the motion effectively delegitimises Israel and stigmatises Jews who identify as Zionists. The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC), the UK regulator responsible for enforcing the Equality Act 2010, received formal complaints alleging unlawful discrimination and has now written to the Greens requesting further information to assess the motion’s practical impact. The party’s leadership, led by Zack Polanski, has defended the motion as a political position that does not affect membership rights, while also pledging to uphold its antisemitism guidance. The controversy arrives at a sensitive moment for the Greens, who are already reeling from a recent by‑election loss and face pressure from Labour, which has threatened to end power‑sharing agreements on local councils unless the motion is repudiated.

analysis.heading: Legal and regulatory dimensions
analysis.content: The EHRC’s intervention is grounded in the Equality Act 2010, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of religion or belief. The regulator’s assessment will focus on whether the motion translates into concrete disadvantages for Jewish members – for example, exclusion from party activities, disciplinary actions, or a hostile environment that could deter participation. Past EHRC investigations have shown that policy statements alone are not automatically unlawful; the key test is the ‘practical effect’. However, the motion’s explicit definition of Zionism as an ideology that seeks domination could be interpreted as a blanket condemnation of a belief held by many Jews, potentially breaching the protected characteristic of religion or belief. If the EHRC finds a breach, it can issue compliance notices, require policy revisions, or, in extreme cases, refer the matter to the courts for enforcement.

analysis.heading: Party politics and electoral consequences
analysis.content: The Greens are a small but increasingly influential force in UK local politics, often entering coalition arrangements with Labour and the Liberal Democrats. Labour’s warning that it will withdraw from power‑sharing unless the Greens disown the motion puts the party’s council representation at risk, especially in areas where Green councillors hold the balance of power. Internally, the motion has split the party: four of five Green MPs and two former leaders publicly condemned it, calling it “dangerous” and “divisive”. Leader Zack Polanski described the motion as “imperfect” and signalled a willingness to amend it, but the party’s constitutional procedures make rapid changes difficult. A prolonged dispute could erode voter confidence, particularly among moderate supporters who view the Greens as a progressive but inclusive alternative to mainstream parties.

analysis.heading: Broader implications for the UK antisemitism debate
analysis.content: The controversy arrives amid a heightened national conversation about antisemitism in British politics, following high‑profile inquiries into Labour’s handling of the issue. The Greens’ motion adds a new dimension by targeting a political ideology rather than overt hate speech, raising questions about the line between legitimate criticism of Israeli policy and discrimination against Jews. If the EHRC rules the motion unlawful, it could set a precedent for how political parties frame debates on Israel‑Palestine, potentially curbing similar language in future party conferences. Conversely, a finding of no breach might embolden other parties to adopt more hard‑line stances, complicating efforts by the government and civil society to combat antisemitism while preserving freedom of expression.

items.outlook: In the short term the Greens face intense pressure to either amend the motion or risk losing critical council partnerships. The EHRC’s investigation, expected to conclude within a few months, will determine whether the motion breaches the Equality Act and could trigger enforcement action. Regardless of the outcome, the episode is likely to fuel broader debates on the limits of political speech concerning Israel‑Palestine, and may prompt other parties to review their own policy language to avoid similar challenges. Labour’s stance suggests that any failure to distance the Greens from the motion could lead to a realignment of left‑wing local alliances ahead of the next general election.

entities.name: Green Party of England and Wales

items.fulltext:
Equality watchdog writes to Greens over 'Zionism is racism' motion
- Published
The equality watchdog has written to the Green Party asking for more information about a controversial "Zionism is racism" motion passed by members.
The Equality and Human Rights Commission (EHRC) said it recognised that "many Jewish people will be feeling vulnerable" following the motion, passed at the party's conference earlier this month.
The motion described Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state in historic Palestine to the exclusion and/or domination of the non-Jewish population".
In a response to the ECHR letter, the party said it "will not discriminate against or exclude people for holding Zionist views" and was committed to tackling antisemitism.
Dozens of Labour and Lib Dem MPs and Jewish campaigners wrote to the regulator raising concerns about antisemitism after the Green motion was passed.
Alongside Jewish groups, the motion was criticised by four of the five Green MPs and two former leaders, one of whom said it was "dangerous" and "divisive".
It piled some pressure on Green leader Zack Polanski in the wake of a by-election defeat. He said the motion was "imperfect" and he wanted to see it amended.
Labour has said it will end power-sharing agreements with the Greens on local councils, unless its councillors disown the motion.
On Thursday, the EHRC confirmed it had written to the Greens following the complaints received.
A spokesperson for the watchdog said: "We have written to the Green Party of England and Wales about its recently adopted 'Zionism is racism' motion to ask for more information and assess its practical implications and potential impact.
"We have received complaints alleging unlawful activity under the Equality Act 2010, including concerns that Jewish people could face discrimination because of their beliefs following the adoption of the motion."
The watchdog said it would "take action where appropriate" after assessing the extra information.
"In the case of the Green Party motion, compliance with the Equality Act is likely to hinge on the practical effects of the motion," the spokesperson added.
In a letter earlier this month, some MPs raised concerns not only about the motion itself but also amendments to protect Jewish Green members at Zionist synagogues being voted down.
"Taken together, these developments raise serious questions about whether Jewish members can participate freely and equally in the party, and whether their religious and communal connections could expose them to complaints or disciplinary action," their letter said.
Separately, the Campaign Against Antisemitism wrote to the EHRC alleging the party had breached the Equality Act through discrimination against Jews.
The campaign group said the motion "effectively states that the state of Israel should not exist" and "defines support for a Jewish homeland in any form as racist".
Having been backed by members, the motion has become party policy but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.
In response to the EHRC letter, the Green Party of England and Wales said it "will not discriminate against or exclude people for holding Zionist views" and the motion sets out a political position with "no impact on membership conditions or internal disciplinary processes".
"The party's comprehensive antisemitism guidance, which forms part of our framework of ethics, remains unchanged," a spokesperson added.
"We remain committed to tackling antisemitism and ensuring Jewish members feel welcome and respected."
